data.title: Colony Bank uses gen AI to shave days off SBA loan approvals
data.description:
• Key insight: Using generative AI helped Colony Bank adapt to new SBA rules more readily, according to an executive at the bank.
  • Forward look: The bank plans to start approving larger loans on the platform in a few weeks.

When the Small Business Administration announced changes to SBA loan requirements in August, Darren Davis, president of Colony Bank's small business specialty lending division, estimated the changes would add five days to the time needed to process each loan, on top of the typical ten-day loan approval process.
The Trump administration issued 416 pages of revised SBA rules that took effect Oct. 1. The new rules tighten lending criteria, increase documentation requirements and alter business acquisition standards.

Davis and other leaders at Georgia-based Colony Bank deployed generative AI-based business loan origination software from Lama AI and were able to reduce the lending process from 92 steps to 32 — a 67% reduction.

"Now if the customer's engaged with us and responsive, we're about seven business days," he said.

Colony now originates all of its SBA Express loans, along with certain other non-SBA commercial loan products, through Lama AI. 

In a broader trend, U.S. banks are seeing productivity gains from implementations of AI. In an American Banker survey conducted earlier this year, 41% of respondents said AI integration was the top driver of improved employee productivity over the last 12 months, followed by improved efficiency internally (34%), new tech and tools (25%), task automation (23%) and process simplification (17%).

In lending, banks are typically using AI in credit decisions to approve more loans. 

"If I'm using AI to say no, then that's questionable, especially under issues like fair lending," said Carey Ransom, managing director of BankTech Ventures. 

At PNC, generative AI is never used to say no on a credit decision, according to Ned Carroll, the bank's head of data and automation. "But I very well might use a generative AI system to say yes more often," he told American Banker in a recent interview.

At Colony Bank, generative AI performs data validation and analysis and makes a recommendation that's reviewed by a human.

The bank started down this path two years ago. "We had a small working capital program," Davis told American Banker. "We had two different tiers on it — up to $150,000 and up to $350,000 — and we were looking for a system that would allow people to get pre-qualified for one or the other before they went into a full application process, and so that was our initial thought on it. When we saw the robustness of Llama, we started going down a different path."

The different path was to use Lama as a full loan origination system, rather than just a front-end solution for initial assessments.

Davis's team used the software to remove 60 manual tasks from the loan process. 

"A lot of our information is document reading and verifying what the customer put in versus what's on a document," he said. "A lot of that went away because Lama does that for us. Lama's able to read documents and populate fields, so we know it's coming from the source and it's not being fat-fingered in. We're not having to double-check to make sure people entered things correctly."

The software compares data provided on loan applications against data from LexisNexis and a third party business scoring provider to conduct know-your-customer and know-your-business data validations. 

Not having to double-check numbers saves an "immense amount of time for our team," Davis said. "It allows us to meet our goal of being able to spend more time on customer relationship building rather than monotonous tasks that really don't further a relationship."

The bank uses a pass-fail underwriting model. Lama "was able to take the information from different sources and understand if it passed that criteria or not," Davis said. "We still want a customer or a human to look at it."

Read more:

  • As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS?
  • Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline
  • Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it
  • Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated

It took two months to roll out the software for the small working capital loan program. 

"We were under the gun because of the SBA rule changes," Davis said. 

Colony has now been using Lama for small working capital loans for about six months and plans to go live on it with larger SBA loans in a couple of weeks. 

The bank makes between 250 and 450 small business loans a year. Davis said the bank can grow its working capital program with fewer people. One person who was processing originations has been moved over to the loan sales side already, he said.

"We're already saving on the gross cost," of SBA loans due to the new software, Davis said. "But once we see the returns down the road, it'll be even more compressive ROI than we have right now."

The bank is preparing to launch SBA Standard on Lama to originate larger business loans in the next couple of weeks.

data.title: How Mike Lyons, Truist's new CEO, is plotting a turnaround
data.description:
• Key insight: Mike Lyons, who took the reins as Truist's CEO last month, announced several changes Friday that he believes will better position the bank for success.
  • What's at stake: The long-struggling superregional bank will need to move relatively quickly to satisfy shareholders, who have been waiting for years for the underperforming bank to deliver on the promises it made seven years ago.

The new chief executive officer of Truist Financial shared his vision Friday for what he believes the underachieving superregional bank can become, and outlined the initial steps it's taking as part of that evolution.

In his first public remarks since joining Truist just over six weeks ago, CEO Mike Lyons told investors that Truist has "all of the raw materials to become one of the country's top-performing banks." Reaching that goal, he said, is the $554 billion-asset bank's "overwhelming No. 1 objective."

Lyons also acknowledged Truist's bumpy history, saying that while it has "an exceptionally strong foundation," the Charlotte, North Carolina-based company hasn't lived up to its potential since being formed seven years ago through a much-criticized merger of equals.

Now it's time for change, starting with new leadership in consumer banking and a reallocation of resources away from underperforming businesses and into those with higher returns, Lyons said. The bank reaffirmed its expectation that it will achieve a key profitability target next year — a 15% return on tangible common equity — and said it's still committed to 16%-18% over the long term.

"While I believe that history and context are important, and we have learned from it, we are where we are today, and we know we can perform better," Lyons said on the bank's third-quarter earnings call. "We're now squarely focused on the future and are fortunate to move forward with some tremendous assets. Importantly, we do not need to reinvent Truist to win from here."

Analysts who cover Truist were quick to point out a change in tone with Lyons in the CEO job.

"Strategically speaking, I absolutely love the contrast in tone at the top," Mike Mayo, an analyst at Wells Fargo Securities, told American Banker. "This is clearly a much more shareholder-oriented CEO," whose earliest message centered on simplifying, executing and growing to create shareholder value, he said.

Still, Lyons and his management team are in a difficult spot, at least in the near term, Mayo said.

"Financially, progress is going to be a slog," Mayo predicted. "They've not been in growth mode, and now they're in shrinking mode. So I do think there will be some earnings headwinds."

Changes afoot

On Friday, the bank said it hired two experienced executives to oversee consumer banking and small business banking, a move designed to increase accountability in each of those segments, and that the previous head of consumer and small-business banking is leaving the company.

It also said it will sell nearly all of the assets of LightStream, the unsecured lending platform it acquired in 2012, to Carlyle Group, marking the bank's latest shift away from non-core lending.

The LightStream deal, which includes $7.7 billion of non-core loans, is expected to close by year-end. It will generate $7.2 billion of net proceeds, which Truist plans to use to repay wholesale borrowings.

Lyons, the former president of PNC Financial Services Group and former CEO of Fiserv, will have to move with urgency to keep shareholders satisfied.

Though he will be granted a window of time to begin shaping Truist into the bank he wants to create, shareholders will be eager to see progress and, in turn, higher returns, said Scott Siefers, an analyst at TD Cowen.

"Virtually everyone I know thinks extraordinarily highly of Mike and what he'll be able to do, but while Mike is new, the story of Truist is not," Siefers told American Banker. "There's a sense that people have been waiting for Truist to reach top speed for a while, and investors probably have some concern that this story will have to take another step back before it can step forward."

Truist is in the midst of a detailed strategic review of each of its businesses, including its lending portfolios, to determine what will help it become a top-performing bank and what's holding it back, Lyons said. The results of that review are expected to be unveiled in early 2027.

So far, the findings are mixed, according to Lyons. The branch network is strong, and there are several high-quality businesses, such as corporate lending, commercial real estate and wealth management, he said. At the same time, "we found capital spread to a lot of areas," including in areas that don't support the bank's core strategy, Lyons said.

"We have a clear lens … Is it strategic? [Are there] clear financial returns? Or does it … do something to protect the bank?" he said. "If it doesn't, we're moving it out."

The bank has already taken certain actions to exit national businesses, as it attempts to focus on its core Southeastern market. In September, it said it would sell $5.5 billion of auto loans, clearing out most of the assets of its auto-lending subsidiary, Regional Acceptance Corp.

In July, prior to Lyons' arrival and soon after setting higher profitability targets, the bank said it stopped originating loans for marine and recreational vehicles. The shift was an effort to drive higher returns, improve efficiency and direct capital to the highest-generating areas of the bank, Bill Rogers, Truist's immediate past CEO, said at the time.

As part of the leadership changes announced Friday, Truist said that Dontá Wilson, who has been Truist's chief consumer and small business banking officer for the past three years, will leave the bank at the end of the year. Wilson, a member of the bank's executive management team, was an executive at BB&T prior to the merger with SunTrust Banks, which created Truist.

In a LinkedIn post Friday, Wilson said he has "deep optimism for Truist's future and great pride" in the bank. He said Truist's employees and clients "are in great hands."

Meanwhile, D. Steve Boland, the former chief administrative officer at Bank of America, is joining Truist as vice chair. Boland, who retired from BofA last year, was BofA's president of retail banking before he was promoted to chief administrative officer.

Boland is set to join Truist on Dec. 1, a Truist spokesperson said Friday in an email.

Shimna Sameer, another longtime BofA executive, will become Truist's chief consumer banking officer. Sameer, who was hired earlier this year to lead Truist's wealth management business, will instead lead the bank's efforts to grow core deposits, deepen primary banking relationships and improve the client experience. She will start on Oct. 19, the Truist spokesperson said.

In addition, Jeff Warner is coming on board later this month to serve as chief small business banking officer. Warner was named head of small business at Pittsburgh-based PNC in December 2024, according to his LinkedIn profile. His 17-year tenure at PNC overlapped with Lyons' time there.

Boland, Sameer and Warner will report directly to Lyons, the bank said.

Rogers is still with the bank, serving as executive chair of the board. He plans to fully retire from Truist in April 2027.

Third-quarter results

Truist's third-quarter results, which were released Friday, were mostly overshadowed by Lyons' first comments as CEO. For the period ending Sept. 30, the bank reported net income of $799 million, a sharp year-over-year decline stemming from a $1.4 billion pre-tax loss on the sale of available-for-sale securities and impacts related to the sale of the auto-lending portfolio.

Excluding those items, net income was $1.4 billion for the quarter, the bank said.

Earnings per share were 56 cents, missing the $1.21 consensus estimate of analysts who were polled by S&P Capital IQ. Total revenue was nearly $3.8 billion, down from about $5.2 billion in the year-ago quarter, while noninterest expenses rose slightly to $3.1 billion as of Sept. 30.

The bank's net interest income rose 0.7% year over year, mostly driven by fixed-asset and liability repricing, higher client deposit balances and higher loan balances, Truist said.

Read more:

  • BofA gets $1.21B penalty for money laundering
  • Wells Fargo HUD probe signals risk for race-based lending
  • Debanking makes a campaign stop in Kentucky
  • Bankers grapple with liability when AI agents mess

Noninterest income dropped 95% compared with the year-ago period, reflecting the $1.4 billion securities loss as well as a decline in mortgage banking fees and "other income," the bank said.

The bank's return on tangible common equity was 7.2% for the quarter, or 14.6% on an adjusted basis.

What Lyons does next, and how he decides to mold Truist, will be critical, Mayo said. It will be a multiyear transformation, Mayo predicted.

"Defining who they don't want to be is sometimes as important as defining what they do want to be," he said.

data.title: Wise on AML: 'It's difficult to get everything right'
data.description:
• Key insight: Wise said it has addressed AML issues in a U.S. consent order. 
  • Expert quote: "We've been investing in compliance in 'know your bank' and 'know your customer' over the past 15 years." —Wise Chief Financial Officer Emmanuel Thomassin

Wise contends it has addressed anti-money laundering concerns but does not have a timeline to resume its quest to receive a bank charter in the U.S.   

 "We have provided the full remediation on every point that was part of the consent order," Emmanuel Thomassin, Wise's CFO, said during the company's earnings call Thursday night.  "We are now waiting for the feedback from the authorities."

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency in July denied Wise's application to charter a de novo U.S. national trust bank, citing deficiencies in the company's Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism program.  In mid-2025, Wise entered into a $4.2 million consent order with six U.S. state regulators over deficiencies in its AML program and suspicious-activity reporting. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) cited Wise for deceptive marketing of ATM fees and remittance violations, resolving the action with an amended order requiring $450,000 in restitution and a civil penalty

This week, Thomassin said that while Wise waits for U.S. regulators to respond to the moves Wise has made to shore up its AML strategy, the timeline to resume its application for a charter is "open." "We've been investing in compliance in 'know your bank' and 'know your customer' over the past 15 years," Thomassin said. "We know our reputation depends on this."

Wise is not alone in facing government pressure over money laundering controls, as Bank of America this week was fined $1.2 billion over AML lapses.

"I can't comment on the other banks, what they are facing, but I think this is a reflection of how difficult it is to get everything right when you do AML," Thomassin said. 

Wise's earnings

For the quarter ending September 30, Wise reported net revenue of $739 million, up 21% over the the same quarter in 2025, with cross border volume growing 22% to $72 billion and customer holdings expanding 28% to $44 billion, Card spending was $14 billion in the quarter, up 30%. Wise raised its revenue growth to the upper half of a 15%-20% range. 

Wise recently moved its primary listing to the U.S., and has focused on expanding its outreach to small to medium sized businesses. Thomassin said the company has formed a dedicated team to engage with business owners.

 "We're reacting to the demand and questions that they may have, and also we also reach out to make sure that they can use in full the servicing that we offer," Thomassin said, adding the strategy differentiates Wise from legacy banks. "The second part of it is, we are getting more and more included in their internal workflow."

Wise is also attempting to compete with large business technology firms by offering an application programming interface that connects directly to small businesses, supporting other functions beyond financial services. "Small businesses may not opt for Oracle or SAP," Thomassin said. In other moves, Wise this quarter went live in Malaysia, launched the Wise Account and Wise Card in Thailand, introduced Wise Assets in New Zealand and announced Wise Platform partnership with OakNorth to support international payments for its U.K. business customers.

"We continued to expand our network, products and features so Wise can serve more people and businesses around the world," Kristo Käärmann, co-founder and chief executive officer of Wise, said in a statement.

'Margin pressure'

Analysts at William Blair noted Wise's commentary suggested broad-based strength across regions and the businesses, with North America being one of the fastest growing regions. 

"That said, the weakening dollar caused some moderation of high-value sends from the U.S. and currency fluctuations may drive continued volatility in reported growth rates," William Blair analysts said in a research note. "Revenue growth should moderate in the second half due to the timing of pricing/investments; however. We anticipate margin pressure in fiscal 2028 due to continued investment, yet we believe management will remain disciplined and view the opportunities from small businesses."

Read more:

  • As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS?
  • Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline
  • Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it
  • Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated

Wise's approach is a self-reinforcing flywheel, William Blair analysts said. "More cross-border volume drives scale benefits and gross profit dollars, which are systematically reinvested in the product, technology, infrastructure, marketing, and price, all of which drive more volume."

data.title: M&T says it's monitoring impact of AI agents on deposits
data.description:
• Key insight: M&T Bank CFO Daryl Bible downplayed the impact that consumers' increasing use of AI agents could have on banks' deposits.
  • What's at stake: Following the recent release of Meta's Muse product, the potential for AI agents to accelerate deposit outflows has become a key topic among bankers and regulators.

A top M&T Bank executive said Friday the bank is monitoring the potential impact of third-party AI agents on deposit flows, but is not concerned about the technology at this point.

Speaking on the Buffalo, New York-based bank's third-quarter earnings call, Chief Financial Officer Daryl Bible said AI agents that are already in use could make it easier for customers to move deposits between institutions to maximize yields. But the bank has yet to see a significant effect on deposit flows, he said.

"We aren't really seeing much impact of actually money being moved out or anything yet," Bible said. He added that M&T is monitoring the situation "very closely."

Bible expects the potential impact to become less significant over time, as the technology matures.

"It's not going to be as much of a big deal," he said.

The potential for AI agents to accelerate deposit outflows has emerged as a recurring topic on third-quarter bank earnings calls and among banking regulators. The conversation kicked off last month following Meta's launch of its Muse agent.

JPMorgan Chase executives addressed the issue Tuesday, saying third-party AI agents do not fundamentally pose new competitive threats to the bank, though they could introduce risks for customers who rely on the tools to manage everyday tasks.

Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Chair Travis Hill also weighed in on Wednesday, saying that while AI agents could make it easier to move money, their adoption does not necessarily mean most bank deposits will leave the system.

"It's something we're certainly watching very closely," Hill said.

Read more:

  • BofA gets $1.21B penalty for money laundering
  • Wells Fargo HUD probe signals risk for race-based lending
  • Debanking makes a campaign stop in Kentucky
  • Bankers grapple with liability when AI agents mess up

Hill said it remains an open question how willing individuals and businesses will be to delegate decisions about moving their money to AI tools. He also noted that businesses account for a significant share of deposits across the banking system and have numerous reasons for choosing particular banking relationships.
In a note Friday, Jaret Seiberg, managing director at TD Cowen, agreed that the risk of consumer-deposit outflows may be limited, but cautioned that regulators should examine the potential implications, as the risks could grow over time.

"What concerns us are not just AI agents. It is the marriage of AI agents with tokenized deposits, tokenized money funds, stable coins, and a potential Open Banking rule that could make it easier for consumers to disintermediate their bank," Seiberg wrote.

Third-quarter earnings

For the third quarter, M&T reported net income of $775 million, down 2% from the same quarter a year earlier. Net interest income rose 1.8% year over year to $1.79 billion.

Average commercial real estate loans and mortgage loans both increased 4% year over year, reaching $24.9 billion and $25.2 billion, respectively.

The growth in average CRE loans reflected strong loan originations in the third quarter, along with stable payoffs and paydowns, Bible said. Average consumer loans rose 5% year over year to $27.3 billion.

Average total deposits increased 2.6% year over year to $166.8 billion, driven by growth in commercial, mortgage and business banking. Bible said deposit growth allowed the bank to reduce its reliance on borrowing. Average short-term borrowings fell $2.8 billion to $5.2 billion.

The bank's provision for credit losses rose by 8% year over year to $135 million, and by 12.5% from the previous quarter.

M&T's net interest margin narrowed to 3.65% in the third quarter, down from 3.69% a year earlier.

Noninterest expenses rose to $1.39 billion from $1.36 billion a year earlier, driven by higher salary and benefit costs and increased spending on outside data processing and software. Software-related costs rose $19 million from the previous quarter, reflecting higher costs associated with software maintenance and enhancements to M&T's technology infrastructure.

data.title: Home equity deal shows VantageScore viable for RMBS ratings
data.description:
• Key Insight: Find out how S&P Global assigned preliminary ratings to a fintech's home equity transaction that used VantageScore 4.0.
  • What's at Stake: Potential for use of more flexible credit measures and digital operations in the private secondary market for home loans.
  • Supporting Data: S&P mapped the 753 weighted average VantageScore for the loan pool, to 742 on the classic FICO scale. Subsequent adjustments in this particular deal lowered it to 737.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. 

A new transaction by Aven is the first deal fully composed of home equity products underwritten using VantageScore to receive ratings from S&P Global's residential mortgage-backed securities team.

"What we tend to see is more adoption in the agency space, less in the non-agency," Jeremy Schneider, managing director and sector lead, RMBS - structured finance told attendees at S&P Global's Affordability Forum 2026 in New York. "But I will say we just issued preliminary ratings today on the securitization of home-equity line cards that uses VantageScore 4.0."

The deal is the first to go through S&P's preliminary rating process with VantageScore 4.0 used to underwrite 100% of the loans, according to the company's report on the transaction, which also shows an alternative to the mortgage industry's standard tri-merge was used.

Other rating agencies may treat transactions with VantageScore, potentially provided with the classic FICOs that have been the mortgage industry's standard, but S&P was able to rate it based on VS4 alone using its methodology, Schneider said in an interview.

The collateral is a participation certificate representing a 100% beneficial interest in a pool of fixed-rate closed-end home equity receivables created under a pool of HELOC credit card accounts. HELOCs are typically considered exempt from ability-to-repay rules.

Home equity lines of credit share similarities with non-mortgage sectors where alternative credit metrics are used more freely. This makes HELOCs a natural way to introduce more use of VantageScore 4.0 as officials modernize credit in government-related mortgage markets.

The preliminary ratings S&P assigned to the Aven transaction, which range from a speculative grade B to the highest-end investment category of AAA, demonstrates the viability of VantageScore's use for at least one type of transaction in the private residential market.

Both alternative credit metrics and how the preliminary ratings treat digital originations, which consumer finance fintechs are increasingly using to handle home equity, also could be significant in a mortgage market with new business opportunities constrained by higher rates.

Adjustments for credit alternatives, digital operations

S&P was able to assign preliminary ratings to the deal through a mapping it uses to correlate VS4 scores with the classic FICO measures that the home mortgage industry has exclusively used until recently. This removes the need to also provide the classic FICO metrics for ratings.

While S&P has said it may need to make rating adjustments in situations where a choice of credit metrics could involve cherry picking, the Aven deal was underwritten conservatively.

The lower of VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 9, a predecessor to the 10T risk model the government-related mortgage markets are moving toward, was used in the Aven deal.

The rating agency did make some other adjustments because trimerged credit reports that have been standard for the residential mortgage industry were not used in the transaction. 

While other consumer finance sectors have used single reports, the mortgage industry has historically had a tri-merge standard with the aim of ensuring decisions about loans used for relatively larger housing transactions are based on sufficient data.

More recently, the Mortgage Bankers Association has pushed for further exploration of whether single report use for higher credit borrowers could cut costs and result in more competition for the three bureaus that back VantageScore without introducing too much risk.

Studies on the matter of whether using fewer than three credit reports for residential loans incurs too much risk have varied, with S&P finding bi-merge outcomes not significantly different from three reports during the Biden administration, when this was favored over a single score.

S&P Global rating analysts applied a haircut of 5 points to each VantageScore before mapping to account for the use of a single credit report rather than a trimerged one.

On a weighted average basis, the VantageScore for the pool before the application of this haircut was 753, which mapped to 742 on the classic FICO scale or 737 with the 5 point haircut.

S&P analysts also included adjustments for its operational assessment of Aven's digital platform, which does not allow for any underwriting exceptions, or physical documentation outside any that certain jurisdictions may require.

"In our analysis of the transaction, we performed an operational assessment of Aven, including a review of the underwriting guidelines which resulted in a loss coverage adjustment factor of 1.050x," the analysts wrote in their preliminary rating report.

data.title: BankThink Green-lighting new banks could help female entrepreneurs raise capital
data.description:
• Key insight: Fintech firms are moving in large numbers to acquire bank charters. This could be very good news for entrepreneurs, especially women and minorities, who are often ignored by more traditional banks.
  • Supporting data: Despite owning 39% of U.S. firms, startups with all-female founding teams received 2.1% of venture capital funding. 
  • What's at stake: Funding constraints hamper business formation, leading fewer entrepreneurs to start enterprises.

Starting a business is not easy, especially when one has the passion but not the finances. 

The vast majority of entrepreneurs do not have access to bank loans or venture capital. Instead, they bootstrap their ventures from income, credit, borrowed resources from loved ones and personal savings. The good news is this is changing: Entrepreneurs are poised to expand their pool of capital funding sources from familiar names in online lending. Affirm, PayPal, Enova and OppFi are part of a wave of financial technology, or fintech, payment companies pursuing pathways to become banks.

Regulators considering applications for fintech and bank mergers or acquisitions must weigh many considerations. However, policymakers should welcome the interest of fintechs in the banking world — one of the most highly regulated industries.

By increasing access to institutional capital — and creating new, faster, more accessible pathways to getting this capital — policymakers can help Americans overcome one of the biggest hurdles to starting and growing enterprises. 

Consider Destyny Dindy, a personal trainer who sought to start her own business. Alternative credit such as small-dollar loans helped her cover expenses between paychecks as she got her business off the ground. Without these financial lifelines, Destyny could not have built her fitness business.

Female and minority entrepreneurs know the challenges of accessing private institutional capital for their startups. Women begin with less capital than men. Despite owning 39% of U.S. firms, startups with all-female founding teams received 2.1% of venture capital funding. 

Racial minorities experience similar capital funding gaps as women. New Black-owned firms start with a third of the capital as their white counterparts and are more likely to use credit cards to fund their startups.

Various factors explain these capital gaps, including borrower risk and investor risk preferences. Borrowers with limited business history and limited assets at start-up may not be able to prove their creditworthiness to secure investment.

Funding constraints have real consequences for our economy. They hamper business formation, leading fewer entrepreneurs to start enterprises. Also, firms launched without institutional capital tend to be smaller, have fewer sales and lower profits, lower employment, and higher failure rates.

The economy needs a healthy and growing banking system. After the Great Recession and the COVID pandemic, banks consolidated, and over 5,000 bank branches closed, leaving many consumers in "banking deserts." At the same time, consumer patterns have shifted to embrace the convenience that mobile banking and digital services provide. 

Read more:

  • Bill would force bank regulators to disclose Epstein records
  • Bowman: Global regulators should match Fed's 'modernization'
  • Fintechs asking for, and receiving, bank charters in 2026
  • Banks face liability over use of AI chatbots, report finds

Still, millions of Americans operate outside of the traditional banking system entirely. According to Federal Reserve data, more than 18% of U.S. households are either unbanked or underbanked. They tend to be young, non-Asian minorities, less educated and residing in low-income households. Traditional banks won't lend to borrowers who might not repay. These high-risk borrowers have low credit scores, high debt-to-income ratios, thin credit histories, unsteady incomes and past financial crises.

Fintechs precisely serve high-risk borrowers. By partnering with traditional banks, fintechs offer them alternative credit or loan products. This system works. Granting fintechs bank charters would allow this industry to serve consumers currently unserved by traditional banks — with a payoff of greater access to credit, potentially at lower costs, and new rewards and products.

Fintechs are often targets of critics on the Left who bemoan their business model as predatory. Lawmakers like Senator Elizabeth Warren are none too happy with fintechs gaining bank licenses and are pressing the Trump administration to halt Enova's charter application. Nearly two dozen state attorneys general called on federal banking regulators to block fintechs from acquiring banks. 

Yet granting fintechs bank charters moves them into full prudential banking supervision — including under the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and possibly the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and Federal Reserve — which critics should welcome. 

Fintechs will have to compete under added restrictions and compliance costs. Regulators will examine fintechs' capital ratios, liquidity buffers, and earnings to ensure safety and soundness. Although fintechs and banks are both subject to anti-money-laundering and terrorist financing laws such as the Bank Secrecy Act, or BSA, and Anti-Money Laundering, or AML, fintechs stand to assume new customer onboarding, compliance, and reporting obligations. In addition, they face consumer-protection requirements and compliance with the Community Reinvestment Act if they take on bank deposits.

States would lose the ability to enact interest rate caps on alternative credit that have proven to restrict access to credit for the riskiest borrowers without improving financial hardships like delinquencies, as the Federal Reserve has proven.

Bringing fintechs under greater banking oversight signals an evolution for this industry that serves those too often forgotten. Aspiring entrepreneurs stand to gain.

data.title: Basel may encourage more nonbank mortgage lenders to go bank
data.description:
• Key takeaway: If proposed changes to bank capital rules take effect as written, some mortgage companies may consider acquiring a bank to diversify their businesses. But industry stakeholders caution that the process can take years, requires significant preparation and does not guarantee regulatory approval. 
  • Expert quote: "The best of intentions in crafting legislation and regulations can sometimes end up with the most unintended consequences." —Tom Piercy, director of MSR advisory at Mortgage Capital Trading

WASHINGTON – Proposed changes to bank capital rules could have the perhaps unintended effect of encouraging more independent mortgage bankers — nonbank mortgage companies known as IMBs — to acquire banks or bank charters.

The proposed modifications to the Basel III capital framework would eliminate the threshold-based deduction for mortgage servicing assets, instead applying a 250% risk weight to all such assets. That change, while subtle, could make bank charters more attractive to IMBs with large servicing portfolios by changing how those assets are treated for regulatory capital purposes.

Although some nonbank mortgage lenders have added banking operations to their businesses, the strategy remains relatively uncommon. Stringent regulatory and liquidity requirements have made obtaining a bank charter difficult and the outcome undesirable for many IMBs.

Tom Piercy, director of MSR advisory at Mortgage Capital Trading, said the proposed Basel changes could expand the role of banks already participating in the mortgage market, but is unlikely to bring many banks in from the sidelines of the market. But it could end up encouraging more nonbank lenders to acquire bank charters, Piercy predicted.

"The best of intentions in crafting legislation and regulations can sometimes end up with the most unintended consequences," said Piercy, who is advising IMBs on pursuing bank charters.

A June paper by the Urban Institute estimates that four to eight IMBs could pursue bank charters over the next five years if the Basel reproposal takes effect. The largest IMBs — among them giants like Rocket Mortgage, United Wholesale Mortgage and PennyMac — may be best positioned to make the transition because of their scale and ability to manage higher funding costs, according to the paper. 

"The elimination of the MSR threshold deduction makes it more feasible for nonbanks in the mortgage space to secure bank charters than it has been in years," the paper argues. "Midsize IMBs with $1 billion to $10 billion in equity can now acquire small to midsize banks for deposit funding and charter access without becoming regulatory-capital insolvent."

A bank charter would allow servicing-heavy IMBs to extract greater financial value from their servicing portfolios by using deposits to fund lending and developing cross-selling opportunities, said Rich Swerbinsky, founder of Onward & Upward Consulting. It would also allow IMBs to tap federal funds via the Federal Home Loan banks.

"Once you're a bank, the servicing book works a lot harder," Swerbinsky said. "Escrow balances become your own cheap deposits instead of sitting at somebody else's bank. Every borrower you service becomes a deposit and cross-sell relationship. And your recapture engine runs on deposits instead of a warehouse line."

Those benefits don't come cheap, however, as banking charters bring with them greater regulatory scrutiny and supervisory hassles — and that's after the considerable burden and uncertainty surrounding obtaining a bank charter in the first place. 

Ari Karen, a partner at Mitchell Sandler, said oversight of nonbanks can vary in scope and frequency, while banks face more consistent regulatory scrutiny.

"Whether it's the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. or the Federal Reserve, you are going to be more regularly audited, and those audits are going to be fairly deep," Karen said. "There's a greater degree of responsibility, particularly if you're going to be dealing with an institution that's insured by taxpayers." 

Karen also added that attaining the bank charter itself requires jumping through a handful of procedural hoops that can take years, including creating a business plan and building out the right management team that is reviewed prior to approval.

Read more:

  • BofA gets $1.21B penalty for money laundering
  • Wells Fargo HUD probe signals risk for race-based lending
  • Debanking makes a campaign stop in Kentucky
  • Bankers grapple with liability when AI agents mess up

The application process can also take years, requiring prospective banks to develop a business plan and assemble a management team that regulators deem qualified to operate a banking institution, Karen said. 

"They're not just going to hand the keys to that car to anybody," said Karen. "Regulators want to see levels of experience in managing these types of businesses. They want to see acceptable risk profiles. They want to see the way you've managed your business."

Still, Karen said clients who have acquired banks have generally been satisfied with the decision. 

Cornerstone Capital Bank is one example of an organization that transitioned from an independent mortgage bank to a bank in 2022 via the acquisition of Roscoe Bank. Adam Laird, CEO of Cornerstone Home Lending, the bank's mortgage division, said the move helped "derisk the organization" by diversifying its revenue streams.

"As just an IMB, there's less diversification in terms of revenue streams, and so you've got greater risk to long-term stability," Laird said. "Our objective at Cornerstone was to build a more diversified platform that has mortgage banking and loan servicing at its core, and then create additional core businesses of commercial banking, institutional banking, insurance."

The transition took years of planning. The process began in 2019 and involved regulatory examinations and stress tests, Laird said. He cautioned that even after completing these steps, a bank charter is not guaranteed. 

Laird said the proposed Basel changes, which are expected to be finalized by the end of the year, could spur greater interest among IMBs in pursuing bank acquisitions. But he cautioned against making such a consequential decision based solely on a regulatory change.

"It's going to take a real strategic commitment," Laird said. "And becoming a bank and the strategic vision to become a bank shouldn't be done just because of a single rule change. It really requires a larger focus on the long term."

data.title: Forget the billionaire tax. This California measure could affect 376K taxpayers
data.description:
• Key insight: While California's proposed billionaire tax has sparked discussion, another statewide proposal on the ballot would make permanent the increase in the top marginal tax rates, which range from 10.3% to 12.3%.
  • Supporting data: Proposition 3 would affect nearly 376,000 taxpayers, compared with roughly 200 individuals who would be affected by Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax.
  • Expert quote: "This should be getting a lot more attention than it is, and I think you will see that pick up in the near term." — Jason Stephens, Evertern Wealth

California's proposed one-time tax on billionaires has dominated much of the midterm tax debate, but another proposal on the ballot this fall would have implications for a far larger group of taxpayers.

Proposition 3 would make permanent California's temporary increase in income tax rates for high earners, currently set to expire in 2031. Those top marginal income tax rates range from 10.3% to 12.3% and apply to income above specific thresholds: $361,000 or more for single filers or $721,000 or more for joint filers. Most of the revenue from the measure would be allocated to K-12 schools and the rest to community colleges.

For advisors with clients in California, the prospect of making these rates permanent raises questions about tax planning, including decisions about residency, Roth conversions, and when to time capital gains and other types of income. If the measure passes, advisors may need to work with clients on rethinking their plans.

Prop. 3 would affect nearly 376,000 individuals, based on 2024 data, while the billionaire tax, Proposition 40, would only affect about 200 Californians, according to the latter measure's proponents.

Polling indicates Prop. 3 is likely to pass. A September survey by the nonprofit, nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 58% of likely voters would support Prop. 3, while 40% would oppose it.

Some wealth advisors are already considering the potential implications for clients.

"If you're a good advisor, you should tell your client they should live the life they want to and not live it around taxes," said Samuel Diarbakerly, the founder and CEO of Boston-based wealth management firm Generation Capital Advisors. "So, if you live in California and Prop. 3 passes, well, you're going to be subject to additional income tax."

In practice, however, some clients are more sensitive to tax increases than others. 

"Now some clients have the prerogative and are principal-bound and say, 'Hey, if I get taxed one more dollar, I am out of here,'" Diarbakerly said. "When you start adding these taxes together, if you're exposed to this, you're probably exposed to the highest, federal marginal rate. You're also probably exposed to the [net investment income] tax."

For clients considering a relocation, advisors should take a family office approach to changing the client's domicile and coordinate with legal and tax counsel, he added.

California residents affected by the tax may not leave the state right away, but the prospect of permanently higher rates could factor into relocation decisions over the coming years.

"This is exactly what a lot of people were talking about where you go after the billionaires, but you end up hitting the millionaires and the people below [that level] with other taxes, and it's a fallout," said Jason Stephens, founder and managing partner at Naples, Florida-based registered investment advisor Evertern Wealth. "So this should be getting a lot more attention than it is, and I think you will see that pick up in the near term, where you will see a lot more people talking about this because it affects, again, significant amount of people compared to the billionaires' tax, which only affects a few people."

How attitudes toward the tax have shifted

Marc Rosenbach, founder and managing partner of Los Angeles-based registered investment advisor Atlas Legacy Advisors, said attitudes toward California's higher income tax rates have evolved since voters first approved the temporary increase in 2012. By 2016, he said, the measure faced more skepticism, though not as much controversy as the current proposal to make the increase permanent.

Now, with permanence on the table, some high earners in the top tax brackets "feel misled," Rosenbach said. He is surprised that Prop. 3 isn't getting more attention, unlike the billionaire tax. 

"Prop. 40 is getting all of the oxygen in the room," he said.

Even if voters approve Prop. 3, Rosenbach doesn't expect a significant change in how he approaches financial planning for clients.

"Because we've been dealing with this since 2012, there's really no change to how we approach our clients," he added. "We approach them with best practices to manage a very high combined tax bracket," often 50% between federal and state.

Even so, he sees a shift in how wealthy Californians  weigh the decision to move out of the state for tax reasons. He said he has seen regret from individuals who have moved away. He now sees some placing greater value on living near family in California than on reducing their taxes.

"It is so easy to have the conversation with a client hypothetically about the present and the future — it's all about the numbers," Rosenbach said. But he tells clients and prospective clients to consider both quantitative and qualitative factors, including "the quality of your life and the roots you've laid down for several decades and understand what it means to be away from that for six months" to avoid being considered residents of California.

"Clearly now that there are enough people who have left, and they're realizing what they've left behind, what they're losing, and how their time on this planet is limited, they're realizing, 'Wait a second. Maybe I'm going to go back to Southern California despite the high tax bracket because I miss my friends and family,'" he said.

data.title: Fed's Warsh to look beyond interest rates over next 100 days
data.description:
• Key insight: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said monetary policy has dominated his focus during his first months at the helm of the central bank, but he said that doesn't mean he's forgotten about the Fed's other duties.
  • Expert quote: "The head of the Fed needs to be head of all parts of the Fed." — Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh

The Federal Reserve's new chair said he has been overly fixated on monetary policy during his first months in office, but that is about to change.

Late Thursday night, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said he intends to spend the next 100 days focusing on the other parts of the central bank, including supervision, regulation and payments processing.

"The head of the Fed needs to be head of all parts of the Fed," Warsh said, noting that only about a quarter of the central bank's staff is focused directly on matters of monetary policy.

Warsh's comments came during an on-stage conversation with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at an IMF event in Bangkok, Thailand. 

Warsh attributed his outsized focus on monetary policy on the exigencies of the current economic moment as well as the voluminous outside attention that interest rates always attract from financial markets. 

Shortly after joining the Fed in May, Warsh announced five task forces to examine different parts of the institution's approach to monetary policymaking, including its balance sheet policy, its use of data, its understanding of productivity and jobs, its assessment of inflation and its communication strategy. 

Warsh said he would take a similar "first principles" approach to other Fed functions, seeking to understand their core objectives to devise the best strategies for them going forward. He noted that all parts of the Fed's operations were critical to its overall credibility.

"Whatever any part of the federal reserve does if they slip up, if they stumble on supervision or on payments, that reflects on our institutional credibility," Warsh said. "So [for] my next hundred days, I'm going to try to give equal focus to those other parts of the business, because they matter too."

"When you take over a position like this you need to lead all of it and you need to love the institution enough across everything they do to ask first principles instead of 'Well, we do it this way because that's how we've always done it,'" he added. "That's not good enough."

Warsh's broadened focus comes at a time of substantial change within other parts of the Fed. After pursuing a series of sweeping regulatory changes, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman is spearheading a restructuring of the central bank's supervisory structure. Meanwhile, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller has discussed the transformative potential that artificial intelligence has for the future of payments. 

Read more:

  • Inflation likely to spark more rate hikes: Boston Fed's Collins
  • Why Citi remains cautious on key profitability metric
  • Goldman's Solomon wants 'clear human accountability' on AI
  • Fed, OCC order Amex to overhaul AML controls, fine $350M

On the topic of monetary policy, Warsh said little about what the Federal Open Market Committee might do later this month, citing his well-established aversion to forward guidance.

Warsh's on-stage appearance came on the heels of a pair of key inflation readings from September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' consumer price index and producer price index, both of which came in higher than expected. Using components of CPI and PPI, the personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed's preferred measure of inflation — is expected to come in around 3% later this month.

For his part, Warsh indicated that he was not surprised by the high readings or any other economic data released since the last FOMC meeting.

"Broadly over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," he said.  

The FOMC increased its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point last month on the grounds that inflation has been too high for too long and is not moving quick enough toward the Fed's 2%. 

Based on the FOMC's quarterly anonymous forecasts and various speeches in recent weeks, the majority of the committee's participants expect to raise interest rates again before the end of the year. The lingering question has been whether that will translate into one quarter-point hike or two.

The Fed chair's comments come on the eve of the Federal Open Market Committee's two-week communications blackout period for FOMC participants that precedes the committee's next meeting on Oct. 27 and 28.

data.title: How 5 of the industry's biggest firms do RIA custody
data.description:
• Key insight: When it comes to custody, the big firms all do it differently, leveraging different aspects and advantages to attract the business of RIA firms.
  • What's at stake: For advisors looking to choose a custodian, factors including name recognition, technology integrations and track records come into play. 
  • Expert quote: "Any custodian you have, I don't care what anyone says, it's going to come with challenges." — Brett Bernstein, CEO of XML Financial Group

Over nearly 30 years in the industry, financial advisor Brett Bernstein has worked for and with some of the biggest names in wealth management. The CEO and co-founder of Bethesda, Maryland-based registered investment advisory firm XML Financial Group first broke into the industry at Merrill and spent a dozen years with LPL Financial before his RIA joined Focus Financial Partners in 2016. Three years later, XML acquired another Focus affiliate that brought its own broker-dealer into the fold, which led to a new relationship with Wells Fargo's First Clearing as the clearing and custody provider to the rebranded brokerage, XML Securities.

Operating a multibillion-dollar RIA that is a wholly owned indirect subsidiary of Focus and uses Fidelity Investments as its custodian, while also running a brokerage that works with the clearing and custody arm of Wells Fargo, can certainly get cumbersome for Bernstein and the team supporting 25 advisors in five offices, he said. But, from his perspective after decades in the industry, those components add up to just the right setup for the team to serve customers at many different stages of investing and levels of complexity across $4.3 billion in client assets. The in-house brokerage and its agreement with First Clearing have also helped smooth the transition of two teams that XML acquired without needing to change the clients' custodian.

"Any custodian you have, I don't care what anyone says, it's going to come with challenges," Bernstein said. "I think Wells Fargo was smart. … They realized it's cheaper to keep the advisors than it is to keep losing them back and forth."

Wells Fargo, LPL, RBC, Raymond James and Goldman Sachs share custodian businesses in common that display a willingness to work with external RIAs in a way that their brethren among the giant brokerages haven't embraced. While their largely undisclosed amounts of assets under custody among RIAs with no registered representatives affiliated with those firms' brokerage or RIA arms likely fall far short of the scale of Fidelity and Charles Schwab, the five companies have built substantial custody businesses among external advisory practices.

Those firms "recognized that they could leverage what they already have in place for outside RIAs to use, without having to reinvent their models completely," according to Jodie Papike, CEO of independent advisor recruiting and executive placement firm Cross-Search.

To be sure, some varying, firm-specific factors led each into serving as custodians to independent RIAs at different times, and name recognition among consumers favors some of the big firms more than the others. At the same time, as the independent RIA channel draws more advisors and clients from wirehouses and other brokerages, the companies that would presumably be in a position to lose that business altogether have developed a method to retain some portion of it through their custodians.

"There are all these different creative ways that firms can put themselves out there to advisors so that, no matter how they want to affiliate with them, they're still a good option to them," Papike said. "The bigger firms tend to be more nimble in how they allow advisors to affiliate with them, and they have the resources to do that."

A varying landscape for custody across the RIA and brokerage world

For this 12th installment of Financial Planning's ongoing series on the fees and business models of the industry's custodians, FP sent questions and interview requests to all five firms, offering the opportunity for any of them to push back against the idea that they belonged in the group. Though they straddle several industry classifications, the firms frequently flex their ability to work with independent RIAs that use their custodians in some capacity without being registered brokerage or investment advisory reps of the firms. That latter regulatory distinction separates the business line from so-called hybrid RIAs that are independent while using a brokerage.

For firms like Merrill, Morgan Stanley and UBS, the custody for external RIAs "means supporting the independent channel their own advisors leave for," according to William Trout, the director of the securities and investments practice with consulting firm Datos Insights, and Gregory O'Gara, a strategic advisor with the firm's wealth management practice. As an example, they pointed to Morgan Stanley's 2021 move to spin off the custodian once known as Trust Company of America, then called E-Trade Advisor Services and now named Axos Advisor Services. Goldman went in the opposite direction when it acquired Folio Financial in 2020. Goldman has been ramping up its RIA recruiting to the point that it even acts as a custodian to the company that acquired onetime aggregator firm United Capital from it in 2023, Creative Planning.

But Wells Fargo has been the exception to its wirehouse peers in its structure, given that the Wells Fargo Advisors Financial Network is one of the largest independent brokerages. Wells Fargo's First Clearing also provides services to TradePMR by Robinhood, and it will be rolling out a specific unit catering to external RIAs later this year, Trout and O'Gara noted. It, LPL, RBC, Raymond James and Goldman each approach RIA custody in slightly dissimilar manners from one another — and distinctively from the three largest custodians in the industry, as well.

"Schwab, Fidelity, and Pershing compete for independent firms on scale, technology, and advisor support," Trout and O'Gara said in an email. "Each of your listed five firms run RIA custody as an extension of a franchise built around its own advisors, clients or products. Goldman treats custody as a distribution channel for capital markets, lending and asset management. Raymond James uses it as a retention tool for advisors who want to go independent. LPL extends a channel it already operates. Vanguard's pending purchase of Altruist points to a different purpose again: vertical integration. Owning a custodian allows an asset manager to reduce its reliance on third-party platforms and the revenue-sharing arrangements that come with them."

How the firms describe it

In keeping with that divergent theme, the five firms differed widely in their responses to FP's questions. Representatives for Raymond James and Goldman did not respond to inquiries.

LPL supplied a link to its standard account and service fee schedule and disclosed that it had $358 billion in independent RIA assets under custody at the end of the second quarter. The company didn't respond, however, to a further request for the specific amount with independent RIAs that do not have any LPL registered reps. Regardless, LPL has been "providing custody, clearing, technology, service and business support to both fee-only RIAs and hybrid RIAs" since 2008, according to Marc Cohen, a group managing director and LPL's chief growth officer.

While Cohen acknowledged in an email that LPL's custodial revenue stems "from multiple sources, including transaction activity, cash sweep, lending interest, product-related economics, and custody or platform fees," he noted that the company doesn't sell proprietary investment products or payment for order flow. And that distinguishes LPL from many wealth management companies that do have those latter two common industry conflicts of interests.

"LPL is an advisor-centric business, and we do not compete for end clients. Financial advisors are our clients, and our focus is on supporting them and helping them grow their businesses," Cohen said. "No matter how advisors choose to structure their business, from independent RIAs to corporate RIA affiliation, hybrid or fee-only models or outsourced operations, LPL provides the flexibility and support to help them achieve their vision. LPL provides the scale of a leading custodian with integrated technology, business support and service capabilities in one ecosystem."

RBC brings an even longer track record of working with external wealth management firms, dating to the launch of RBC Clearing & Custody in 1979. Representatives with the firm noted in an email statement that it is the custodian to more than 300 firms "in the U.S. and in select global markets, including breakaway advisors, start-ups, wealth management firms, money managers, dually registered firms and institutional-based firms." The representatives cited the "depth and consistency of our service," as well as "the financial strength of our parent company" and the firm's technology resources.

"Our Minneapolis-based technology team supports every aspect of the technology experience: strategic consulting for well-informed technology decisions, tactical implementation for customizing a firm's tech stack, training and support for faster adoption and greater productivity, and data analytics support for regulatory compliance and business insights," RBC's statement to FP said. "Many factors play into our overall pricing. Each firm we partner with has a unique business model and business plan, giving us the opportunity to tailor pricing. We see the relationship as a commitment to our clients' success and our focus stays on delivering value aimed at helping them meet their goals."

Wells Fargo's First Clearing has maintained such relationships with external independent brokerages and RIAs for roughly 40 years, according to an interview with Erik Karanik, head of independent solutions with Wells Fargo's Wealth and Investment Management division and Leann Markovitz, who is head of First Clearing. Those services will enter a new phase in early December, with the launch of Wells Fargo's new RIA Solutions unit.

While the firm also opened an RIA channel in 2019 under its collaboration with TradePMR, the new program will deliver the services entirely through Wells Fargo as a third leg of its independent advisor businesses, alongside FiNet and First Clearing. The latest outreach reflects the "market trends" that continue to see advisors moving to RIAs, Karanik said.

"We think we have the capacity to serve the advisors along the spectrum, where they can garner more control of their businesses, more control of their client experience and we want to provide the scale and support to provide those client solutions," he said. "To have the RIA Solutions was a logical next step."

He and Markovitz declined to share any metrics for the size of First Clearing's custody business, but Karanik said that it is comparable to that of Apex Fintech Solutions in "the next tier" below Schwab, Fidelity and BNY Pershing. In terms of fees, First Clearing doesn't share any schedule publicly, but the rates are based on criteria such as an advisory practice's business model, requirements and use of the custodian's services, Markovitz said.

"Through due diligence and the capabilities that they need, we work with those firms to price that business," she said. "We look at the needs of the firm to price that business."

An RIA-by-RIA fight for custody

Those kinds of negotiations play out regularly for custodian sales teams at RIAs across the country such as Synergy Financial Group, a San Ramon, California-based firm with nearly $1 billion in client assets. The firm has always worked with multiple custodians, according to Synergy Chief of Staff Shannon Irwin. However, after months of due diligence and meetings, she and the rest of Synergy's team switched one of its custodial relationships at the beginning of the year to Goldman from Pershing while keeping its agreement with Schwab, Irwin noted.

While she said she wouldn't describe them as "unhappy" with Pershing over anything in particular, Goldman's private wealth and banking capabilities brought "additional benefits we wanted to award our ultrahigh net worth clients," Irwin said. Goldman won out by identifying more areas of value it could deliver to the firm's customers, and the fees represented only one aspect of the decision.

"We are very transparent with our clients, so fees obviously are something that we take into consideration," Irwin said. "They took the time to understand our business, because that's something that is really important to us."

Simpler transitions often play a role in advisors' decisions as well, although the significance of that factor can shift over time. When Franklin, Tennessee-based SageSpring Wealth Partners and its president, Jeffrey Dobyns, dropped Raymond James Financial Services in late 2024, he left "a lot of good friends at Raymond James," where they "were super kind to me," Dobyns said. But the technology, favorable fee rates and flexibility of working with multiple custodians in Schwab and Fidelity won out over the idea of retaining Raymond James as a custody provider.

"The nice thing was it was easy," Dobyns said. "The bad news was, the economics were still not really competitive."

Brand name, technology and track record could all enter the mix of advisors' decisions, according to Bernstein of XML. RIAs will be comparing, say, the draw and product access of a name like Goldman to rivals like Schwab, Fidelity, Pershing, First Clearing and LPL.

"The answer is, can you compete enough and bring me something that others can't?" Bernstein said. "Nine times out of 10 the lawn turns brown, so you really have to believe that grass is going to be green for your clients and your team."

data.title: Schwab blocks unauthorized AI agents, points clients to 'Charley'
data.description:
• Key insight: Firms like Schwab and JPMorgan are blocking third-party AI agents from accessing client accounts out of security concerns.
  • What's at stake: Some say the real fear is third-party AI agents could automatically sweep uninvested cash out of low-yield brokerage accounts into higher-yielding investments, threatening billions in net interest revenue.
  • Expert quote: "An outside agent works for the client. Charley works for Schwab." — Tim Welsh, Nexus Strategies

A little over a month after Meta released its Muse AI assistant capable of performing financial and other tasks, Charles Schwab says it's blocking outside agents from accessing its clients' accounts.

Instead, Schwab is directing clients to its own fledgling AI assistant, Charley, while also allowing them to use ChatGPT and other large language models for stock trades and other transactions. In an earnings call Thursday, Schwab CEO Rick Wurster portrayed the decision to block outside AI agents as necessary for protecting client data.

Schwab is specifically preventing AI agents from using clients' login credentials or browser automation to access its systems.

"In terms of (large language models), we want to deliver AI to clients in a safe and secure way," Wurster said. "And there's one way we think is not safe, and that's just an agent coming to our site and trying to log in on behalf of a client. We are not going to allow that." 

Rise of the AI agents

Wurster wasn't the only CEO to discuss in an earnings call this week possible security threats posed by autonomous AI agents. On Tuesday, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon told analysts that he and his fellow executive aren't going to allow just any "outside agent to come in inside the company, because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan."  

Wurster and Dimon's comments come a little over a month after Facebook parent Meta released its Muse agent. Muse and other AI assistants stand out from ChatGPT and other LLMs in their ability not just to answer questions but to perform complex tasks on their own. Muse, for instance, can be directed to make online purchases autonomously and draw up financial reports and budgets.

One step it's not allowed to take, though, is to move money in or out of banks or brokerages without getting the account owner's permission. But even without that authority, security experts worry that autonomous agents with access to a large variety of online accounts can put client data at risk.

Wurster said Thursday that he receives notice every time Schwab has to block an agent driven by AI. The reports are few and far between because most clients "aren't using it in that way in their financial life."

Schwab counters with 'Charley' AI assistant

Rather than outside agents, Schwab is directing investors to its Charley AI assistant. Wurster said Charley will initially be able to take only a few actions on clients' behalf, "like changing an address or naming a trusted contact."  

Charley, which will be introduced in coming months, is built atop various outside LLMs and Schwab's own data. Now its main use is for "information and synthesis," Wurster said.

He said Schwab meanwhile also allows traders to use certain LLMs to connect to Schwab and complete transactions. More clients and LLMs will eventually be given the ability to trade but not to "move money, because we think there's too much risk there to the client and to the firm," Wurster said.

"So we have two opportunities, whether it's coming in through … your own LLM or coming in through Charley," Wurster said.

Over time, Wurster predicted, Charley will become an "important front door to Schwab."

The AI assistant will "give you the full range of things you can do on schwab.com and be able to do anything through a conversation via either text or voice," Wurster said. "And I expect, over time, it will be the primary way to connect to AI at Schwab."

How AI could threaten Schwab's cash-sweeps revenue

Tim Welsh, the founder of the consulting firm Nexus Strategies, said the concerns about protecting clients' data are no doubt real. But Schwab, he said, clearly has an incentive to prevent AI agents from infringing on business it wants to keep for itself.

"An outside agent works for the client," Welsh said. "Charley works for Schwab."

Industry analysts in recent months have noted the threat Muse and other AI agents could pose to Schwab and other brokerages' lucrative business handling clients' cash. Through a process known as cash sweeps, many firms move uninvested cash sitting in brokerage accounts over to banks and then keep a large percentage of the interest generated from lending it out.

AI agents put all that at risk because of their potential to ensure cash is automatically being moved into higher-yielding investments. The hit to brokerages' bottom lines could be sizable.

Schwab, for instance, reported on Thursday that it made nearly $3.48 billion in net interest revenue in the third quarter, much of it on nearly $493 billion held in cash-sweeps accounts.

"Ultimately, this is about cash," Welsh said. "Schwab earns a lot on client cash sitting in low-yield sweeps. An independent AI agent's first job would be to find that cash and move it somewhere that pays more." 

Like many brokerage executives, Wurster has been quick to downplay the supposed threats from AI. On Thursday, he said he and his colleagues are finding clients who use AI to help them make trades are entrusting more cash to Schwab.

"I know one of the fears in the market about us is that as AI takes off it will impact cash levels," he said. "We're actually seeing the opposite impact, that the more people use AI, the more cash they hold because they're more active in buying stocks."

Schwab uses AI to haul in net new assets

Schwab is one of many firms looking for novel uses of AI. Last month, Schwab announced that the tech giant Anthropic's Claude for Advisors AI assistant is being made available to the more than 16,000 independent RIAs that receive support through its Schwab Advisor Services division.

Wurster said Thursday that AI is also helping Schwab with goals like bringing in assets from new and existing clients. Schwab's haul for net new assets — excluding market gains and assets from one-off events like acquisitions — was $190.4 billion in the third quarter.

That was up 38% year over year and marked a record high for the firm in the July-to-September period. Wurster said Schwab's financial consultants and other client-facing professionals have various AI systems at their disposal.

"I think that is also part of what's driving our [net new assets], part of what's allowing us to have richer conversations about their wealth and driving some of the growth in our wealth and lending capabilities," he said.

He said most of the fastest growing source of new assets was in-house advisors that Schwab refers to as financial consultants, "which is why we continue to invest in new branches and adding client-facing professionals." Schwab recently took out an advertisement in the Wall Street Journal saying it was planning to add thousands of financial consultants to its current stable of roughly 3,000. 

Schwab's asset inflows were just one aspect of a generally strong quarter for the firm. Its net revenue was up by 17% to nearly $7.2 billion and its net income by 23% to $2.9 billion. Its pre-tax profit margin — revenue left over minus expenses other than taxes — was 3.5 percentage points year over year to 52.7%.
