data.title: Amid pessimistic economic and policy sentiments, advisors see the potential in their firms
data.description:
• Key insight: Advisors are less optimistic in October than they were in the summer about the state of the economy.
  • Supporting data: In a survey of 213 advisors, outlooks and confidence fell more than they rose.
  • Forward look: Despite the worries, advisors reported confidence in their practices.

The optimism of the summer has faded as financial advisors' outlooks on the economy have dipped once again.

After upbeat findings in July, financial advisors' overall outlooks have dropped to their lowest overall level since April in Financial Planning's latest Financial Advisor Confidence Outlook (FACO) survey.  

Outlooks on the global economic system and overall economy, which drove optimism in July, have cooled. Outlooks on government policies and client risk tolerance also fell while confidence in practice performance rose. Advisor confidence fell in October to a score of minus-2 on a scale from minus-100 (most pessimistic) to 100 (most optimistic). That score — compiled from surveys of 213 advisors in October — fell from plus-4 in July. 

Optimism back then was fueled by the economy as the global economic system score rose 17 points to minus-34 from minus-51 in June. Advisors had their eyes on potential geopolitical improvements as concerns related to Iran and the Strait of Hormuz looked to be fading. These newest results come as FACO's schedule has shifted from a monthly to a quarterly report. 

Economic worry remained

Similar to July, the economy was the primary driver of advisors' outlooks in October, but in this instance, outlooks fell substantially. The global economic system score fell 16 points from minus-34 to minus-50, erasing most of the ground it had gained in July, landing the score near October 2025's level of minus-51.Advisors also expect volatility to remain. Fifty-four percent expect the global economic system to experience more volatility over the coming three months, up from 43% in July while 43% expect it to stay the same and 4% expect less volatility, down from 9% in July.

The overall economy also declined by 11 points over the past three months, falling from plus-38 in July to plus-27 in October.

In the survey, 14% of advisors expect the economy to contract, up from 10% in July, while 41% expect it will grow, down from 48%. Overall, more advisors (45%) expect it to remain constant, up from 42% in July.

Sentiment on policy waned

Advisors expressed uncertainty in October around policy issues, which included new legislation and monetary policy with independent RIAs the most pessimistic, scoring minus-22 compared with minus-1 for everyone else in the survey. 

The government policy score fell by 12 points from plus-5 to minus-7, representing its first negative score since June 2024 and its lowest since May 2024.Monetary policy was the biggest reason for the decline. Twenty-one percent of advisors expect a positive impact from it on clients' financial well-being over the coming three months, and 33% expect a negative impact. 

When asked about attitudes around client risk tolerance, 58% expect it to stay the same over the coming three months, compared with 67% in July, while 26% expect a decrease, compared with 19% in July. Expectations that it would increase rose 2 percentage points to 16% from 14%.

The bright spot?

Despite the uncertainty over some aspects of the survey, advisors remained upbeat when it came to their own practices.

Practice performance scored plus-35, rising 9 points and representing the highest score since May, when it was 39. Some 38% of advisors expect their firm will outperform its goals over the next three months, 60% anticipate meeting them and 3% said they expect to underperform. 

Among advisors, those using commission payment structures had more confidence in their practice with a score of plus-54 compared with advisors who don't use commission at plus-21.

data.title: Why some banks are exploring 'bring your own AI agent'
data.description:
• Key insight: Bank of America, BBVA, Synchrony, and Wells Fargo have joined the Personal Agent Protocol, a framework that allows companies to set parameters for what AI agents can do. 
  • What's at stake: Personal agents are growing in popularity, which has spurred some banks to rethink their stance on allowing third-party agents into their systems. 

Banks have been grappling with liability questions surrounding AI agents, but the rise of personal assistants is spurring some to rethink their stance on allowing third-party agents into their systems.

It's called "bring your own agent." The idea is that consumers will largely choose which AI agent they prefer to use on a day-to-day basis, and companies — including banks and retailers — should have systems in place that allow for those agents to connect with their infrastructure.

Some financial services companies already allow for that. Robinhood lets its customers connect their preferred large language model into its own model context protocol, and Coinbase also allows consumers to connect their Coinbase accounts directly to AI assistants for trading and payments.

Others have taken a less accommodative approach. JPMorganChase, for example, has said that it would block third-party AI agents from accessing its systems. Amazon has also said it would block third-party agents.

But as personal AI assistants such as Meta's Muse and Instinct continue to grow in popularity, a small group of banks, including Bank of America , BBVA, Synchrony, and Wells Fargo are exploring a framework that will allow them to set parameters for what an AI agent can do within their systems.

The Personal Agent Protocol, or Poppy, is an open standard backed by Stripe, Sierra.AI, Walmart, Shopify, Meta and personal agent provider Instinct with 35 other design partners, including Target, OpenAI, PayPal, Visa, Mastercard, Adyen and Chime.

"Poppy is built on the principle that customers decide what access to give their personal agents, and companies set parameters for what those agents can do," according to Sierra.AI. "This enables companies to work with personal agents in the way that is best for their customers: through their existing websites and APIs, or through an agent of their own."

The protocol is in its infancy, but it signals that banks are exploring ways to allow third-party agents into their ecosystem, according to Richard Crone, CEO of Crone Consulting.

"The banks aren't going to just limit themselves to their own proprietary AI. They are going to recognize that the consumer is going to want to bring their preferred agent," Crone told American Banker.

Consumers have been receptive to personal AI agents because it is highly personalized and has a horizontal view of what consumers do across every website, Crone said. As of September 19, Meta Muse had reached 2.5 million cumulative downloads across all platforms in the US since its launch on September 8, according to Bank of America Global Research.

There's also a financial incentive for banks and retailers to allow consumers to bring in their own AI agents — specifically in the cost of tokens, Crone said.

"Let's say [Walmart's AI agent] Sparky is wildly successful, or if [Bank of America] was able to update Erica using Anthropic, the token cost will bury them," Crone said. Crone Consulting estimates that an agentic banking session would use between 15,000 and 50,000 tokens per session.

"The only way to do this is to delegate that cost to the consumer's own LLM. Bank of America didn't buy you a cell phone, and they didn't pay for your data plan when they launched mobile banking," Crone said.

But opening banks' doors to third-party AI agents is a massive risk, especially as banks face heightened scrutiny for the actions of their own chat bots.

Still, banks need to find a way to work with other AI agents, according to Kaue Tozzi, global head of product strategy and partnerships at Temenos.

"For a lot of financial institutions, the first agentic payments have most likely already happened at their bank — they just don't know about it," Tozzi said. "It's important that they hyper focus on making sure that they're ready for what's coming 1,2, 3 years down the line, and not waiting to take action until then."

It's also important that banks consider how they want to offer agentic experiences, Tozzi said.

"Ultimately, when something goes wrong, the bank is the bearer of trust, and customers are going to call their bank… when something goes wrong," he said.

data.title: With rates sky-high, mortgages drag down banks' earnings
data.description:
• Key insight: As borrowing to buy or refinance a home becomes less attractive, mortgage lending is suffering at many big banks.
  • Supporting data: At PNC Financial Services Group, quarterly noninterest income from mortgages was down 16% year over year.

As mortgage rates soar, many banks are feeling the pain in their residential loan portfolios — and at least one is trying to offload some of the dead weight.

First Horizon Corp., the Memphis-based parent company of First Horizon Bank, announced Thursday that it is selling about $4.5 billion of "lower yielding" residential mortgage loans. The sale is expected to close in the fourth quarter.

During the bank's third-quarter earnings call, executives said the sale is part of a broader plan to focus on deeper client relationships.

"This transaction … is aligned with the strategy we have discussed consistently throughout the past year of prioritizing full client relationships, enhancing the profitability of our balance sheet and driving improved earnings and returns through the cycle," said First Horizon CEO Bryan Jordan.

But the sale also reflects a simple truth: Mortgage rates have been very high in recent years — particularly last quarter, when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years — and high rates are bad news for the business of originating mortgage loans.

By the end of September, the average rate for a 30-year mortgage was more than 7%, according to Freddie Mac.

The Mortgage Bankers Association recently said that for the week ending Oct. 2, its index measuring borrowing for home purchases was down 15% from the same period a year earlier. Its index measuring refinancing activity was down 56% on a year-over-year basis.

"Very few homeowners have an incentive to refinance at these rates, and the jump in borrowing costs has caused many potential borrowers to step back from the purchase market," Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association, said in a press release.

In the third quarter, Wells Fargo's home lending earnings were down 15% from the year before. U.S. Bancorp's mortgage banking revenue was down nearly 14%. And at PNC Financial Services Group , noninterest income from residential and commercial mortgages was down 16%.

In fact, during PNC's earnings call on Thursday, the bank cited residential mortgages as a reason why its consumer loans declined by 1% from the previous quarter — a rare dark spot in an otherwise strong earnings report.

When asked for a line-by-line forecast of fee income in the fourth quarter, PNC's chief financial officer said he expected the mortgage category to decline.

"Mortgage isn't a big category for us, but obviously, given where rates are … that'll be down," CFO Rob Reilly said.

Similarly, Bank of America saw its average residential mortgage loans in its consumer-banking segment fall to $115 billion in the third quarter, down from $117 billion one year before. During an earnings call on Wednesday, BofA executives said rising rates are hurting its mortgage business.

"Generally speaking, we tend to benefit a lot from the fact that we're really big in credit, mortgages and [municipal bonds]," CFO Alastair Borthwick said during BofA's earnings call. "It just happens that when rates go up 85 basis points in a quarter, that tends not to be good for those businesses."

During First Horizon's call, when Jordan was asked to explain the timing of the $4.5 billion sale, he pointed to the same reason.

"The 'why now' is, it became clear that we're in a cycle of rising interest rates," the CEO said.

In terms of commercial real estate, however, Jordan saw growing opportunities for lending — especially for multifamily homes.

"With what consumers are dealing with right now on top of elevated home prices and higher interest rates, renting is relatively more attractive than buying," Jordan said.

data.title: Citizens' payment exec on how banks can coexist with fintechs
data.description:
• Key insight: Payments veteran Matt Valente has joined Citizens to help lead business payments and partnerships. 
  • Expert quote: "Embedded finance for us is central to meeting clients where they are. It's the best of both the banking and fintech worlds."---Matt Valente, Citizens. 

As banks and fintechs battle for business banking revenue, Citizens' Matt Valente says there will always be an advantage for merchants in having access to a traditional bank.
"You can have a point solution from a fintech. But when you can offer a breadth, such as lock box, ACH, cards, payments and banking, there's a strength in that,"  Valente told American Banker. 

Valente in early October was appointed senior vice president and head of strategy, innovation and partnerships for Citizens, responsible for helping the bank develop products for treasury and wholesale payments. Those duties include technology development, where, like most banks, Citizens is weighing when to compete with or partner with fintechs. There is space for both options, he said. 

"As we evaluate where there are gaps, there will be areas where we'll want to invest and there will be a partner option," Valente said. "That is what we're taking to the executive teams and the bank's board." 

Embedded opportunity

One area where there are opportunities to collaborate with tech firms is in embedded payments and finance, or placing a checkout function directly within a non-financial app. Valente said the bank will seek to mix its own work on embedded payments with technology partnerships. The banking industry in general is lagging merchant demand for embedded payments and embedded finance, creating opportunity for payment fintechs to step into the market. 

Citizens recently developed an open banking application programming interface to support data sharing between customers and third parties, a key element in supporting embedded finance. It also launched account-migration capabilities within its mobile app to let customers move billing, subscription, and payroll information from other institutions. Other banks are also using embedded payments to broaden their appeal to businesses. Huntington, for example, recently partnered with fintech Payabli to support embedded payments, to help Payab-li counter fintechs such as Ramp and Brex, which also sell to businesses. 

And among larger banks, Truist recently signed a deal with data technology firm Plaid to expand the bank's open banking strategy, including more products and security controls. 

"Embedded finance for us is central to meeting clients where they are," Valente said. "It's the best of both the banking and fintech worlds."

More tech

Valente has started his new job at Citizens amid several initiatives designed to keep the bank competitive in digital assets, AI and international payments.

Citizens has spent the past year building infrastructure and products before it rolls out new bank products to corporate clients in 2027, with cross-border payments and money movement, especially in emerging market corridors, being among the first uses. 

It's part of a broader transformation initiative called "Reimagine the Bank" that includes deploying generative AI, AI agents and enterprise automation to reduce manual work involved in data collection, improve ties between vendor contracts and desired outcome, automate call centers and introduce advisory tools. Citizens projects that by late 2028, "reimagine" will produce $450 million in benefits, with two thirds coming from cost savings and the rest from new revenue. 

In digital assets, Citizens recently joined Open Standard's Open USD stablecoin consortium alongside nearly a dozen U.S. banks. Citizens is preparing to test corporate digital-asset use cases in 2027, including cross-border payments, emerging market remittances, digital wallets and interoperability between decentralized ledgers and traditional corporate structure.

Analysts have praised Citizens' technology investments. Analysts at Raymond James, for example, in a research note said Citizens' "Reimaging the Bank" is contributing to an improvement in the bank's overall financial performance, which is "expected to support positive operating leverage and narrow the profitability gap against peers."

Competition

Before joining Citizens, Valente was most recently at FIS, where he was senior vice president of corporate strategy, covering banking, payments and capital markets. He also held several leadership positions at JPMorganChase, including API strategy, open banking, trade finance, payment modernization and commercial banking. 

"I come from both the bank and fintech worlds and the competition has always been there," he said.

  • Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline
  • Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it
  • Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated

In some ways banks are on the defensive when countering fintech influence.For example, banks are lagging fintechs in AI development. While fintechs make up 40% of the data set of recent McKinsey research on AI projects in financial services, they make up 70% of the AI initiatives. 

"Despite their scale and data advantages, incumbent banks trail fintechs in deploying AI with measurable business impact," said McKinsey, which studied 4,000 banks and fintechs.

data.title: Illinois swipe fee case enters the appeals phase
data.description:
• Key insight: Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul plans to appeal a federal judge's decision to block enforcement of parts of the Illinois Interchange Fee Prohibition Act against banks and credit unions.
  • Forward look: Banking and credit union groups are seeking an expedited appeal, saying a swift resolution would help financial institutions determine whether they must incur potentially steep costs to comply with the law.

WASHINGTON — Banks and credit unions notched a victory earlier this summer against an Illinois law barring swipe fees on taxes and tips — but they can't rest easy just yet. 

Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul last week filed a document that said he intends to appeal the court's previous decision to grant an injunction to bank and credit union groups that exempts them from a law limiting swipe fees on tax-and-tip-portions of transactions. State and national groups representing the industries have fought the law for years, saying that it creates an unworkable situation for them, because the current infrastructure for card purchases can't isolate just an interchange fee on only the taxes or tip of a purchase. 

The Illinois Bankers Association, American Bankers Association and America's Credit Unions and Illinois Credit Union League are involved in the lawsuit against the state. The groups filed a cross-appeal after Raoul's office said it would seek to have the injunction reversed. 

Judge Virginia Kendall of the U.S. District Court for the North District of Illinois in June ruled that federal law preempts part of the state's law, and enjoined enforcement against national banks, federal savings associations covered out-of-state-banks and payment networks. In September, she added credit unions to the list. The court ordered Raoul to submit his brief for the appeal by Nov. 23. 

The industry groups asked for a speedy resolution of the appeal. 

"During the course of this litigation, financial institutions and other 

payment-system participants have faced a shifting landscape as the District 

Court, the Illinois legislature, and relevant federal regulators have taken 

actions affecting the nature and timing of their obligations," according to the industry motion.  "A swift disposition of this appeal will bring needed finality to this dispute and allow affected  financial institutions to determine whether they must indeed incur the  'staggering' costs required for compliance with the IFPA."  

The attorney general's office said it opposes the request for expedited treatment. 

"In these circumstances, there is no reason to expedite supplemental 

briefing, oral argument, or this court's consideration of the issues raised in 

the parties' earlier briefs and any supplemental briefs,"  the attorney general requested, according to a court filing.

data.title: While embedding AI 'everywhere,' BNY won't disclose costs
data.description:
• Key insight: BNY, which has leaned heavily into AI in recent years, was reluctant Thursday to say how much it's spending on the technology.
  • What's at stake: Analysts and industry observers are looking for proof that banks' investments in AI will pay off in the form of financial gains.

The Bank of New York Mellon said Thursday that it's embedding artificial intelligence into every corner of its business. What it didn't say is how much money it's spending on AI.
Analysts attempted to extract those details during the custody bank's third-quarter earnings call, but BNY CEO Robin Vince didn't provide a dollar figure. Instead, he talked about the rationale for investing in AI — saying it offers the opportunity to improve outcomes, create capacity and deliver for clients — and arguing that the dollars being spent are generating returns.

The sidestep was hardly surprising. As banks have implemented AI capabilities across their platforms, bank executives have largely deflected analysts' questions about AI-related expenses and returns on investments, saying it's too early in the cycle to provide concrete numbers.

Industry observers have been trying to get a handle on the amount of money that banks are pouring into AI, and whether the investments are producing gains. At BNY, "the answer to the question is yes, we're generating returns, and yes, we want to lean in more," Vince said during the call.

Of BNY's annual $13 billion expense base, about $4 billion is spent on technology, Vince said. 

Regarding the cost of AI specifically, "we're not breaking it out, but it sort of folds into the inputs across our expense base," Vince said. "And frankly, we think it could be counterproductive to break it out and to start obsessing about it publicly and even within the company as an input."

During the bank's second-quarter call in July, Chief Financial Officer Dermot McDonogh offered a slightly meatier response to a question about AI spending. 

"Within the context of $4 billion, AI spend is quite de minimis and quite modest and appropriate for the strategy we have in place," he said at the time.

BNY has championed AI for years. A year ago, it said it had 117 AI solutions in production. That number is now at "400-plus," Vince said Thursday. The bank views AI as a way to increase capacity within its workforce, freeing people up to take care of other tasks, not as a way to reduce headcount, he added.

"We've got plenty of things to do, and so whenever we can generate capacity to provide for that growth without having to grow the expense base, that's phenomenal," Vince said.

Vince's comments followed another strong quarter for the $484 billion-asset bank. It reported firmwide revenues of $5.7 billion, an increase of 12% year over year. Earnings per share totaled $2.34, beating the $2.27 consensus estimate of analysts who were polled by S&P Capital IQ. 

Net income came in at $1.7 billion, up 16% compared with the year-ago quarter. Net interest income rose 15%, primarily as a result of reinvestment of investment securities at higher yields along with balance sheet growth. The increase was partly offset by deposit margin compression. 

Noninterest expenses rose 8% compared with the prior-year quarter to $3.5 billion as of Sept. 30. The company's results included $1 million in provisions for credit losses. The latest return on tangible common equity was 29%, exceeding the medium-term target of 28% that BNY set in January.

Against the backdrop of positive results, BNY once again made upward revisions to its financial outlook for the year. It now expects 2026 revenue to increase 12%-13%, excluding notable items. It had most recently expected revenue to grow 10%-11% from the prior year. Meanwhile, it expects full-year net interest income to rise 15%, a sharp increase from the 10% previously projected.

BNY also expects expenses to rise between 7%-8% year over year, excluding notable items, mostly as a result of higher revenues. In July, it said full-year expenses were expected to rise 6%-7%, excluding notable items.

During the quarter, BNY repurchased $937 million of common shares and paid out $436 billion in dividends.

data.title: U.S. Bank downsizes mortgages in bid to boost fees, deposits
data.description:
• Key insight: Home loans amounted to about 28% of U.S. Bancorp's total loans on Sept. 30, down from 30% at year end 2025.
  • Expert quote: "Where you get fee revenue, you get deep relationships, you get sticky deposits. That's where we want to extend our balance sheet." — CEO Gunjan Kedia

U.S. Bancorp is growing its loans, and as that expansion unfolds, the composition of its portfolio is changing.

The $703-billion-asset superregional is leaning into commercial real estate, commercial-and-industrial and credit-card loans, viewing those sectors as prime avenues for driving increased deposits and fee income. And as it does so, the relative contribution made by its mortgage-lending operation is expected to shrink over time. The bank's executives also indicated Thursday that auto lending will not be as big an emphasis.

"When we started the year, I believe residential mortgage loans were in the 30% area in terms of loan mix," Chief Financial Officer John Stern told analysts on a call discussing U.S. Bancorp's third-quarter results. "We do see that coming down, more because of the growth in the other categories. We do anticipate mortgages will probably be in the mid-twenties at some point."

U.S. Bancorp, the parent company of U.S. Bank, held $116.8 billion of mortgage loans on Sept. 30. That total amounted to 28% of the Minneapolis-based company's $415.2 billion of total loans. Home loans made up just under 30% of total loans at Dec. 31, 2025.

Card loans, C&I loans and CRE loans give U.S. Bancorp better opportunities to capture fees and deposits, along with spread income, CEO Gunjan Kedia said on the conference call.

"Where you get fee revenue, you get deep relationships, you get sticky deposits. That's where we want to extend our balance sheet," Kedia said.

Stern echoed that point in an interview with American Banker. "We think [the card-C&I-CRE emphasis] is a good usage of the balance sheet," he said. "It can be levered into deposit gathering, as well as fee categories."

Both Kedia and Stern emphasized that U.S. Bancorp has no plans to exit mortgage or auto lending.

"It doesn't mean we give up on mortgage or auto, or anything like that," Stern said in the interview. "We still offer those products. We still think they're an important part of the consumer's life cycle, but it's clear where our focus is."

Another bank's approach

Memphis-based First Horizon Corp.'s pursuit of a similar strategy is taking a more dramatic shape. On Thursday, the $84.3 billion-asset bank announced plans to sell $4.5 billion in consumer mortgages and deploy the capital into higher-yielding loan types, including CRE and C&I loans.

"The intent there was mainly to create capacity on our balance sheet to fund continued growth and investing in longer, deeper relationship opportunities that we see in the marketplace," Bryan Jordan, First Horizon's chairman and CEO, told analysts.

Jordan termed the mortgages First Horizon is selling "essentially non-relationship portfolio assets."

Due to the loan sale, which is expected to close in the fourth quarter, First Horizon reported a third-quarter loss of $94 million. But Jordan said the loan sale would be accretive going forward, as First Horizon converts the proceeds into higher-earning assets.

Third-quarter results

For its part, U.S. Bancorp reported net income totaling $2.2 billion for the quarter ended Sept. 30, up 10% from the same period last year. The company reported record quarterly revenue of $8 billion, driven in large part by a 13% year-over-year increase in fee income, which totaled $3.48 billion. Net interest income increased, too, though at a less-robust 5.6% clip.

Loans totaled $415.2 billion on Sept. 30, up 8.6% from a year earlier. Deposits of $531.7 billion were up 1%.

Capital-markets revenue of $640 million spiked 69% from the third quarter of 2025, boosted by the first full quarter of results from San Francisco-based investment bank BTIG, which U.S. Bancorp acquired June 1.

Credit-card loans totaled $40 billion on Sept. 30, more than an 11% year-over-year increase, reflecting the impact of a new partnership with Amazon. U.S. Bancorp began issuing Amazon's small-business credit cards in May.

  • Solid consumer results at Wells Fargo propel larger profits
  • Impostors got past First Horizon's help desk, suits allege
  • BofA gets $1.21B penalty for money laundering

Credit quality remained solid. Nonperforming loans totaled $1.28 billion on Sept. 30, down 20% from the same time last year. Third-quarter net chargeoffs of $523 million amounted to 0.51% of average loans, down from 0.56% for the third quarter of 2025.
While the company is keeping a watchful eye on asset quality, especially in the wake of the recent interest-rate hike, it hasn't detected any signs of deterioration in either commercial lending or consumer lending, Stern said on the conference call.

Jefferies analyst David Chiaverini described U.S. Bancorp's numbers as "solid." Gerard Cassidy, who covers the bank for RBC Capital Markets, described them as "strong."

Investors appeared to be in a similar frame of mind. Shares in U.S. Bancorp were trading up more than 2% at $57.54 on Thursday afternoon.
